Augmenting Long-term Memory

By Michael Nielsen

One day in the mid-1980s, a newspaper reporter named Solomon Shereshevsky arrived at the office of the Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Luria. Luria's story is remarkable, and it raises a question worth taking seriously about the value of memory for creative work.

This essay is about using computers to help us remember. It describes a spaced-repetition system that makes memory a choice rather than a haphazard event left to chance. That shift, from accident to intention, changes what a person can reasonably expect to know.

The role of memory in creative work

Internalized knowledge greatly increases the number of associations available during thought. You cannot connect ideas you do not know, and looking things up interrupts the flow that creative association depends upon.

Isolated questions tend to become orphans: difficult to remember and of little use, because they lack connections to anything else the reader understands. Better to approach an important idea from several related directions.

Practical principles

Make most questions atomic. Asking several things at once leads to unreliable recall and questions that are painful to review over many years.

  • Do not try to remember everything you read.
  • Use the system to understand, not merely to memorize trivia.
